newsitem.title: USA: NY Consumer Board seeks to oppose utility suit.
newsitem.headline: NY Consumer Board seeks to oppose utility suit.

text.p: The New York State Consumer Protection Board has asked the state Supreme Court in Albany for permission to intervene in the lawsuit filed by the Energy Association and seven of New York's electric utilities challenging the State Public Service Commission's proposal to destructure the industry.
The board said the case will be heard before Justice Joseph Harris on October 24.

The utilities filed September 18 saying they did so to preserve their right to challenge the commission's May 20 decision that set the ground rules for future competition in New York's electric industry.

The Consumer Protection Board, through its chairman and executive director Timothy S. Carey, filed papers Tuesday to support the Commission in the Competitive Opportunities lawsuit filed by the Energy Association and its electric utility members.

The electric utilities are Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corp, Consolidated Edison Co of New York Inc, Long Island Lighting Co, New York State Electric & Gas Corp, Niagara Mohawk Power Corp, Orange and Rockland Utilities Inc and Rochester Gas and Electric Corp.
The state Consumer Protection Board was created by the state legislature in 1970 to represent the interests of consumers before the Public Service Commission and other state and federal agencies.

Commenting on the utilities suit, Carey said, "To say that in filing this court case they want to preserve their rights is nothing more than a facade, a smokescreen designed to delay dealing with the reality of electric competition and choice."
He said the board estimates that "for every day there is a delay in moving to competition, New York state ratepayers are foregoing up to $5.6 million in savings."
That's "up to $2 billion a year," he pointed out.

Carey told Reuters the utilities have "taken a gamble" that the courts will agree with them on stranded costs, or prior investments they have made in generation and other costs, that may not be recoverable in a competitive market.
"Stranded costs could be disallowed by the court," he pointed out.

"We think the utilities may have overreacted in bringing this lawsuit," said Carey. "So far, the PSC has not disallowed one penny of prudent stranded costs. In fact, the PSC carefully noted that the utilities would be afforded a reasonable opportunity to recover such costs consistent with the goals of lowering rates, fostering economic development and maintaining reliable service.

"Our view is that the PSC has posed a proper challenge to the utilities to get their costs more in line with what they should be. If they can meet the PSC's goals, no stranded costs may be disallowed. The ball is clearly in their court."
